sections.html:
No. Tennessee's inheritance tax is gone for anyone who died in 2016 or after. The levy is no longer imposed after December 31, 2015, and families should not file for those later deaths.

Back when it applied, the tax reached the portion of the net estate above an exemption tied to the year of death. Net estate meant the market value of every asset after subtracting items such as property passing to a surviving spouse, debts and administration costs, and the executor, administrator or trustee paid the bill from estate funds. A family listing an inherited house in Tennessee today skips that return entirely. The federal estate tax is the only one left, and it reaches very large estates.

sections.h2: When the federal estate tax reaches a Tennessee estate
sections.html:
Only at a very high threshold. The Working Families Tax Cuts law, Public Law 119-21 signed July 4, 2025, lifts the basic exclusion amount to $15,000,000 for 2026. Recent years looked like this:

Year of deathBasic exclusion amount
2023$12,920,000
2024$13,610,000
2025$13,990,000
2026$15,000,000

The top bracket rate has stood at 40 percent since 2013. A typical Tennessee family house falls far under these numbers, so most estates never send a Form 706. Total the house with bank balances, retirement accounts and insurance owned at death before deciding no return is needed.

sections.h2: Carrying over a spouse's unused federal amount
sections.html:
Yes. For decedents with a surviving spouse, an estate may elect, starting January 1, 2011, to pass the decedent's unused exclusion to that spouse. The election sits on a timely filed estate tax return, so a Form 706 can pay off even where no tax is owed.

Simplified valuation rules cover estates that would not need to file apart from the election. A surviving spouse in Tennessee who plans to sell the family home and hold a large portfolio should raise this with the estate's lawyer well ahead of the filing deadline.

sections.h2: Which value heirs use when they sell an inherited house
sections.html:
They use the home's worth at the owner's death. Inherited property generally takes its market value on that day, or on the alternate valuation date if the executor picked one. Any federal gain is measured from that figure, whatever the decedent paid decades earlier, so a sale close to the date-of-death value leaves little to tax.

  • An estate that had to file a federal return gives each beneficiary a Schedule A (Form 8971) stating the estate tax value.
  • Final IRS regulations call for consistent basis reporting between an estate and a person acquiring property from it.
  • An estate under the filing requirement should skip Form 8971, since sending it can produce needless IRS letters.

For a smaller estate, hire an appraiser to value the house as of the death and keep that report with the estate file.

sections.h2: What if a child gave the house to a parent shortly before the parent died?
sections.html:
The rule changes in this narrow case. A special rule carves out appreciated property that you or your spouse handed to the decedent during the final year of life; the death-day value does not govern it. When it comes back to you, your basis equals the decedent's adjusted basis immediately before death.

Appreciated property means an item whose market value on the day of the gift beat the giver's adjusted basis. Tennessee families who retitle a house to a relative and then inherit it back should talk with the estate's attorney first, so the tax effect is clear before anyone signs a deed.

sections.h2: Recording tax when the estate sells the house
sections.html:
The buyer owes it, as the grantee. The county register of deeds collects the recordation tax, and the rate for realty transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 of purchase price.

Property tax follows separate steps. The county assessor appraises the parcel, the county commission and city governing bodies fix rates, and the county trustee and city officials collect. Request the parcel's open balance from the trustee's office and pass it to the closing agent.

sections.h2: County property tax on an inherited house
sections.html:
The assessor applies a 25 percent ratio to residential appraisals to reach the assessed value. Appraisals reset during reappraisal programs on a 6, 5 or 4 year cycle and generally hold steady between them unless buildings change.

  • An owner can challenge an overstated value, an understated value on someone else's parcel, or the way the parcel is classified.
  • The dollar amount of the bill is not a basis for an appeal.
  • The sequence runs from a conversation with the assessor to the county equalization board, which opens its sessions June 1, and on to the state board and Chancery Court.

An heir who receives an older house last appraised years ago may see a new number at the next reappraisal.

sections.h2: How an estate house sale moves along
sections.html:
The order of events is usually the same. First, the court names the person who can sign for the estate, and the clerk issues certified copies of that paperwork. Second, the family gets the date-of-death appraisal and the newest tax bill. Third, the trustee's office gives a payoff number for any open property tax, and any lender gives a payoff statement for a mortgage. Fourth, the title company checks that the signer has enough authority and prepares the closing papers.

At closing, the open tax balance and any loan come out of the sale price, the buyer pays the recording tax when the deed is filed, and the rest goes to the estate. A cash buyer can skip the appraisal and lender steps that a financed buyer needs, which can shorten the wait for the heirs. The estate still needs the same court paperwork either way.

A tidy folder shortens closing and supports the basis you report later. Assemble these before the sign goes up.

  • A certified death certificate and the court order naming the person authorized to sign the deed.
  • The appraisal as of the death, or the Schedule A if a Form 706 was filed.
  • The newest tax bill, plus a payoff number from the trustee.
  • Receipts for additions the decedent paid for, because the IRS counts improvements that add value toward basis.
  • A payoff statement from any lender.

Give the title company copies early so the closer can tell whether the signer needs more authority than the folder shows. Missing court paperwork is a common reason an estate closing slips by days or weeks, so ask the clerk for certified copies in advance.

A taxable gain can call for estimated tax payments, so ask the preparer about due dates once an offer is accepted.

Two items can come up. The IRS fee for an estate tax closing letter, Letter 627, is now $76, up from $56, and it matters only to estates that filed a Form 706. The yearly gift exclusion is $19,000 per recipient for 2026, which can matter if a parent was moving the house to children before death.

On the court side, ask the clerk where the decedent lived which office handles letters of administration or probate of a will. That office can explain what the court must approve before a sale.

faqs.q: Does Tennessee charge inheritance tax in 2026?
faqs.a: No. The tax ended after December 31, 2015, and no return is due for deaths in 2016 or later.

faqs.q: What federal estate tax threshold applies this year?
faqs.a: For deaths in 2026 the basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000 per person, under Public Law 119-21. A surviving spouse can add the unused portion through an election on a timely filed return.

faqs.q: What starting value do heirs use for an inherited house?
faqs.a: Generally what the house was worth on the day the owner died. Any gain is measured from that figure.

faqs.q: Who pays the deed tax on an estate sale?
faqs.a: The buyer pays $0.37 for each $100 of price when the deed is filed with the register.

faqs.q: Can heirs contest the county's value of an inherited house?
faqs.a: Yes, for a value set too high or a wrong classification. Talk to the assessor first, then take it to the county equalization board, which opens June 1.
